spark.summary: High-Level Design (HLD) translates product requirements and scale targets (QPS, p99 latency, durability, RPO/RTO) into a cohesive topology of edge gateways, stateless compute, caches, async queues, and partitioned data stores. Good HLD explicitly isolates failure domains and separates read/write bottlenecks.
spark.keyTakeaway: Start every HLD from back-of-the-envelope QPS, payload size, and consistency bounds, then decouple read-heavy paths with caches/CDNs and bursty writes with durable queues.

concept.whyItMatters: Prematurely jumping into database schemas or class diagrams misses the systemic bottlenecks—hot-key thundering herds, cross-region replication lag, and cascading retry storms—that actually cause production outages and 10x cloud bills.
whenToUse: Designing new distributed systems or major platform migrations (>1,000 QPS, multi-region availability, or strict p99 < 100 ms SLOs).
Architecture reviews and RFCs where teams must align on component boundaries, data ownership, and failure blast radius before writing code.
Principal/Staff system design evaluations requiring end-to-end trade-offs across compute, storage, caching, and async messaging.
whenNotToUse: Early-stage MVPs or internal CRUD tools (<50 QPS) where a single modular monolith + managed PostgreSQL handles years of growth.
Low-level class/interface design (LLD) inside a single service—HLD stops at service boundaries, APIs, and data-flow contracts.
Micro-optimizing CPU cache lines or lock-free data structures before verifying network and storage I/O bottlenecks.
keyPoints: Quantify traffic early: compute read/write QPS (peak = 3–5x average), daily storage growth, and network egress before picking databases.
Separate **stateless compute** (horizontally scalable behind L7 load balancers) from **stateful tiers** (sharded DBs, distributed caches, object stores).
Apply **CQRS** and **async decoupling** (Kafka/SQS + outbox pattern) when write latency, fan-out, or third-party webhooks would otherwise block user-facing threads.
Design for **graceful degradation**: circuit breakers, adaptive concurrency limits, idempotency keys, and stale-while-revalidate caches prevent partial failures from becoming total outages.
Define **RPO** (acceptable data loss) and **RTO** (acceptable recovery time) per tier—active-active multi-region is 3x more complex and costly than active-passive.

examples.title: Flash-Sale E-Commerce Checkout (50,000 Peak QPS)
examples.scenario: A sneaker drop drives 50,000 concurrent users to `GET /product` and `POST /checkout`, risking PostgreSQL connection exhaustion and overselling limited inventory.
examples.outcome: Static product pages are served from CloudFront/CDN + Redis (`<5 ms`), inventory decrements use atomic Redis Lua scripts with a token-bucket waiting room, and confirmed orders flow asynchronously via Kafka into sharded PostgreSQL.

examples.title: Global URL Shortener & Analytics Pipeline (100:1 Read/Write Ratio)
examples.scenario: A link platform handles 1,000 writes/sec (`POST /shorten`) and 100,000 redirects/sec (`GET /:code`) with <20 ms global p99 latency.
examples.outcome: Write path generates 7-char Base62 keys via a ZooKeeper/etcd range allocator into DynamoDB; read path hits edge CDN + regional Redis clusters (99% hit rate), while click events stream to Kafka → ClickHouse asynchronously.

tradeOffs.pro: CP stores (Spanner, CockroachDB, single-leader Postgres) prevent double-spending and stale reads on financial ledgers.
tradeOffs.con: Cross-AZ/cross-region consensus adds 10–150 ms write latency and halts writes during minority network partitions.

tradeOffs.pro: Independent deployments, isolated scaling (GPU inference vs. lightweight API), and clear team ownership.
tradeOffs.con: Network serialization overhead, distributed transactions (Sagas), and operational complexity of service mesh + observability.

tradeOffs.factor: Push (Fan-out on Write) vs. Pull (Fan-out on Read)
tradeOffs.pro: Fan-out on write pre-computes timelines in Redis, delivering <15 ms feed reads.
tradeOffs.con: Celebrity accounts with 10M followers trigger massive write amplification; hybrid push-for-regular / pull-for-celebrities is required.

failureModes.name: Retry Storm / Metastable Failure
failureModes.description: A transient DB slowdown causes clients and upstream services to retry 3x immediately, tripling load on the struggling DB and locking the system in a permanent brownout even after traffic drops.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce exponential backoff with full jitter, per-client retry budgets (max 10% retry ratio in Envoy), and circuit breakers.

failureModes.name: Hot-Key / Celebrity Partition Skew
failureModes.description: Sharding by `tenant_id` or `product_id` sends 40% of total cluster QPS to a single Redis or DynamoDB partition during a viral event, saturating one node while 99 others sit idle.
failureModes.mitigation: Add local in-memory L1 caches (5-second TTL), split hot keys with random suffixes (`key#0..9`), or enable read-replica fan-out.

failureModes.name: Dual-Write Inconsistency (DB + Kafka)
failureModes.description: A service commits a row to PostgreSQL and then crashes before publishing the `OrderCreated` event to Kafka, leaving downstream search and billing permanently out of sync.
failureModes.mitigation: Use the **Transactional Outbox Pattern**: write the event into an `outbox` table inside the same DB transaction and tail it with Debezium CDC.

failureModes.name: Thundering Herd on Cache Expiration
failureModes.description: A popular cached key expires simultaneously for 5,000 concurrent requests, slamming the origin database with identical expensive queries.
failureModes.mitigation: Use request coalescing (`singleflight`), probabilistic early expiration, or serve stale cache values while refreshing asynchronously.

commonMistakes: Designing an architecture without first calculating read/write QPS, payload sizes, and 5-year storage capacity.
Using a single primary RDBMS for both OLTP transactions and heavy analytical `GROUP BY` reporting queries.
Omitting idempotency keys on mutating endpoints (`POST /payments`), causing duplicate charges when mobile clients retry on flaky networks.
Assuming synchronous REST/gRPC chains of 6+ services can achieve 99.99% availability (`0.999^6 = 99.4%` composite availability).
Drawing an 'API Gateway -> Microservices -> Database' box diagram without specifying partitioning keys, caching eviction, or backpressure.

sections.content:
## The idea

High-Level Design (HLD) is the blueprint of how traffic, state, and failures flow through a distributed system. Rather than prescribing individual classes, HLD defines **service boundaries, data ownership, communication patterns (sync vs. async), and scaling axes**.

Every scalable HLD rests on three levers: **(1) Shedding or caching reads** as close to the user as possible (CDN → Edge → Redis → Read Replicas), **(2) Absorbing write spikes** through durable logs (Kafka/SQS) and partitioned storage (hash/range sharding), and **(3) Bounding blast radius** via cell-based isolation, timeouts, and backpressure so one degraded dependency cannot take down the entire platform.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider designing a multi-tenant **Notification & Webhook Delivery Platform** handling 20,000 events/sec:

1. **Edge & Ingestion**: Clients call `POST /v1/notifications` with an `Idempotency-Key`. Envoy terminates TLS, enforces per-tenant token-bucket rate limits, and routes to stateless `ingest-api` pods.
2. **Deduplication & Durable Acceptance**: `ingest-api` checks Redis (`SETNX idem:<key> EX 86400`), validates the payload, writes an `ACCEPTED` record to a Kafka `notifications.inbound` topic (partitioned by `tenant_id`), and returns `202 Accepted` in <15 ms.
3. **Routing & Fan-out**: Stateless `router-workers` consume from Kafka, look up tenant preferences (cached in Redis, backed by PostgreSQL), and route to channel-specific topics (`email.send`, `webhook.deliver`).
4. **Isolated Delivery & Backpressure**: `webhook-workers` execute outbound HTTP POSTs with strict 3-second timeouts. If a customer's webhook endpoint returns `503`, the worker routes the message to tiered retry topics (`retry-1m`, `retry-15m`, `dlq`) without blocking healthy tenants.

sections.content:
## Capacity estimation & partitioning keys

Before selecting technologies, anchor the design in numbers: **QPS** (e.g., `100M DAU × 20 actions/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 23,150 avg QPS`, `× 3 = ~70,000 peak QPS`), **Bandwidth** (`70k × 2 KB = 140 MB/s`), and **Storage** (`2B records/day × 500 B = 1 TB/day`, `365 TB/year` before compression/TTL).

Partitioning keys dictate whether that scale holds. Hash partitioning (`hash(user_id) % N`) spreads writes evenly across shards but makes range scans (`created_at BETWEEN ...`) scatter-gather across all nodes. Range or composite keys (`(tenant_id, created_at)`) support fast time-series queries while risking hot shards for whale tenants—which you mitigate with shard-splitting or salting.

## Storage & messaging building blocks

| Component | Consistency / Model | Throughput Profile | Latency (p99) | Primary HLD Use Case |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **PostgreSQL (Sharded/Citus)** | ACID, Relational | 5k–30k TPS per shard | 5–20 ms | Financial ledgers, user/tenant metadata, strong joins |
| **DynamoDB / Cassandra** | Tunable AP / Key-Value | 100k–1M+ OPS (horizontal) | 3–15 ms | High-velocity writes, time-bucketed feeds, session state |
| **Redis Cluster** | In-memory (async repl) | 100k+ OPS per shard | <1–3 ms | Look-aside cache, rate limiting, leaderboards, locks |
| **Apache Kafka** | Partitioned commit log | 100 MB/s–10 GB/s | 5–25 ms | Event backbone, CDC, CQRS, traffic spike buffering |
| **ClickHouse** | Columnar OLAP | Millions of rows/sec ingest | 50–300 ms | Real-time analytics, clickstreams, observability logs |

## Failure modes

**1. Split-Brain Under Network Partition**: Two database nodes both believe they are primary after a flaky AZ link, accepting conflicting writes. Always enforce quorum-based fencing (Raft/Paxos) or STONITH/lease-based leader election.

**2. Unbounded Queue Lag (Consumer Starvation)**: A downstream dependency slows down from 10 ms to 2 s, causing Kafka consumer lag to grow to 50M messages. By the time it recovers, messages are hours stale and TTLs expire. Enforce **shedding/load-dropping** or **priority queues** (interactive vs. bulk).

**3. Cross-Region Failover Thundering Herd**: Failing over 100% of traffic to a cold secondary region whose Redis caches are empty sends 100% cache-miss load straight to the secondary DB. Pre-warm caches or keep active-active regional cells sized for 50% headroom.

## Resilience, observability & cell-based isolation

At high scale, **cell-based architecture** (bulkheading) limits the blast radius of bad config pushes or noisy neighbors: partition users into independent cells (each holding 5–10% of traffic with its own compute, Redis, and DB shard) behind a thin L7 routing layer. A poisoned query in Cell 3 cannot impact Cells 1–20.

Every network hop must declare **strict timeouts** (shorter than caller deadline), **circuit breakers** (trip at >50% 5xx over 10s), **hedged requests** (only for idempotent reads at p99), and **distributed tracing** so bottlenecks are visible in real time.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Document peak read/write QPS, payload size, p99 latency SLO, and RPO/RTO targets before choosing components.
- [ ] Enforce `Idempotency-Key` headers on all non-idempotent `POST`/`PATCH` APIs.
- [ ] Place timeouts, jittered exponential backoff, and retry budgets on every outbound network call.
- [ ] Separate OLTP databases from OLAP analytics via CDC (Debezium → Kafka → ClickHouse/BigQuery).
- [ ] Verify sharding/partition keys against your top 1% 'celebrity' or 'whale' tenants to prevent hot-shard saturation.
- [ ] Test failover and cache-cold recovery in staging via periodic chaos/game-day drills.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: System Design Hld Architectures

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: High-Level Design (HLD) translates product requirements and scale targets (QPS, p99 latency, durability, RPO/RTO) into a cohesive topology of edge gateways, stateless compute, caches, async queues, and partitioned data stores. Good HLD explicitly isolates failure domains and separates read/write bottlenecks.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Redis + Kafka Backbone applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Sharded DB & Workers.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Sharded DB & Workers experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Enforce exponential backoff with full jitter, per-client retry budgets (max 10% retry ratio in Envoy), and circuit breakers.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Start every HLD from back-of-the-envelope QPS, payload size, and consistency bounds, then decouple read-heavy paths with caches/CDNs and bursty writes with durable queues.
Avoid trap: Designing an architecture without first calculating read/write QPS, payload sizes, and 5-year storage capacity.
Avoid trap: Using a single primary RDBMS for both OLTP transactions and heavy analytical `GROUP BY` reporting queries.
When to reach for it: Designing new distributed systems or major platform migrations (>1,000 QPS, multi-region availability, or strict p99 < 100 ms SLOs).
When to reach for it: Architecture reviews and RFCs where teams must align on component boundaries, data ownership, and failure blast radius before writing code.

putItTogether.title: Putting System Design Hld Architectures Together
putItTogether.summary: Start every HLD from back-of-the-envelope QPS, payload size, and consistency bounds, then decouple read-heavy paths with caches/CDNs and bursty writes with durable queues.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for System Design Hld Architectures before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Static product pages are served from CloudFront/CDN + Redis (`<5 ms`), inventory decrements use atomic Redis Lua scripts with a token-bucket waiting room, and confirmed orders flow asynchronously via Kafka into sharded PostgreSQL.
